title: Xiaomi's Three-Chip Blitz: Trading Resources for Time, Betting on an Edge-AI Paradigm Shift
dek: Xiaomi released three Xuanjie chips in one go, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking and an all-AI architecture — trading resources for time, wagering on an edge-AI paradigm shift and vertical integration capability, though a clear gap remains to the top chip companies.
why: This deep-dive parses the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips with high information density, especially offering clear metaphors for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking. Worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors watching Xiaomi.
who: Investors watching Xiaomi's chip efforts, chip industry engineers, product managers, and tech professionals who want to understand the edge-AI trend.
skip: The first 3 minutes of discussion about the definition of self-development can be skipped; go straight to the technical analysis.

points.h: Whether a company can make chips depends on system definition power, not IP self-development rate
points.body: Judging whether a company can make chips isn't just about how many IPs it hand-built, but how much system definition power it holds. Although Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, system integration and physical implementation are its own. Apple and Qualcomm are strong because they can iterate every year and keep taping out — exactly what latecomers lack most. Xiaomi doesn't have ten years to learn slowly, so it chose an aggressive route, pushing multiple high-risk technology lines simultaneously.

points.h: The culprit behind O1's unideal efficiency is the lack of a shared water tank
points.body: Xuanjie O1 lacks a system-level cache (SLC), so GPU power draw can't be contained under high load, and efficiency is unideal. SLC is like a shared water tank for a neighborhood: the closer data is to compute units, the faster the access and the lower the power. O1's GPU has many cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores wait for data and utilization stays low — this is the bandwidth wall. O3 adds a 16MB SLC, split into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, and designs an on-chip network scheduling system to solve data consistency and access conflicts.

points.h: ARM's public bus is too generic, so Xuanjie had to build its own
points.body: ARM's public CHI+CMN solution is too generic, requiring compatibility and redundancy designs that are hard to customize for Xuanjie. O3 simply developed its own X-Ring unified fusion bus, compatible with CHI but defining its own interconnect protocol, with a self-developed high-speed road network scheduling center and memory controller. This means fewer protocol conversions, and data can decide cache location and path based on demand. Xiaomi data claims protocol conversion overhead reduced by 75%, static access latency of 82 nanoseconds, 32% lower than O1, even lower than Apple A19 Pro.

points.h: The compute bottleneck is shifting from matrix multiplication to vector operations
points.body: O3 adds an AI unit to every subsystem — CPU, GPU, ISP — letting computation happen where the data is, reducing data movement. NPU core count drops from 6 to 4, but Tensor compute rises to 200Tops, because Xiaomi judges that the large-model bottleneck is expanding from matrix multiplication to vector operations such as Softmax, quantization, KVCache, etc. The vector unit area is about the same as Tensor, with 6.8 times the number of multiply-accumulate units as O1, and introduces an SMT-like architecture, similar to CUDA, to handle irregular parallel tasks.

points.h: Chips and models should be defined together by the same company
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with MEMO, using a 5-value quantization method to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits with almost no precision loss, reducing memory bandwidth and capacity demand by 30%. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model deployed on O3 improves prefill performance by 40% and decode by 45%. This ability to jointly define chips and models is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration — no need to wait for others to define a model and then adapt.

points.h: 3nm performance is squeezed out bit by bit from standard cells
points.body: O3 uses the more mature N3P process, improving performance by 5% at the same power, and reducing power by 5%-10% at the same frequency. Xiaomi also did extensive process optimization: self-developed standard cells increased from 480 in O1 to over 2,400, covering all chip units; compressing the power supply buffer channel so power and signals run through the middle of the module, increasing transistor density by 5%. CPU changed from 4 clusters to 3 clusters of 10 all-big cores, with single-core performance up 31%, multi-core up 60%, surpassing A19 Pro.

points.h: Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
points.body: Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking, with one compute wafer and two memory wafers stacked vertically, interconnected via Hybrid Bonding, forming a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical connections to achieve high bandwidth, with lower energy per bit shifted, similar to HBM on mobile. Data: 28,762 data connections, bandwidth 1.22TB/s, far exceeding the tens-of-bits-wide connections of traditional SoC and LPDDR. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each with a RISC-V processor for control.

points.h: ChangXin's value isn't in speed grades, but in joint definition
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with ChangXin to debut LPDDR6, reducing dependence on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if ChangXin offers a starting grade of 10.667Gbps, Xiaomi can compensate for peak speed gaps through wider channels, larger SLC, and self-developed memory controllers. More importantly, the two sides jointly verify and tune from the design stage, jointly defining China's mobile memory subsystem solution. For ChangXin, it proves its high-speed IO and physical layer capabilities, earning a seat at the new-generation mobile memory table.

points.h: Xiaomi isn't betting on chips, but on a time window
points.body: First, betting on an edge-computing paradigm shift: AI's weight in SoCs is growing, phones become the AI interaction entry point, and Xiaomi wants to be in the definer's position. Second, betting that vertical integration becomes the core competitiveness of terminal companies: generic chips can hardly meet the fragmented needs of people-car-home full scenarios, so one must master one's own compute architecture. Third, betting on an uncertain time window, trading resources for time, compressing the technology catch-up cycle, preferring to bear engineering risks rather than wait for the window to close.

points.h: Xuanjie is catching up faster, but hasn't passed any of the three thresholds
points.body: A top SoC company needs three capabilities: self-developed CPU/GPU microarchitecture, self-developed 5G baseband, and continuous multi-generation stable tape-outs with tens of millions of shipments. Xuanjie currently satisfies none, still with a clear gap to the first tier, just catching up faster. What truly changes the industry landscape isn't a single stunning chip, but a group of companies building sustained iteration capability. Xuanjie's greater significance is proving Xiaomi's chip efforts haven't stopped, and it's starting to move forward together with Chinese chip industry partners.

terms.def: A cache shared by multiple compute units within a chip, like a shared water tank for a neighborhood.
A wafer-level 3D stacking interconnect technology that connects directly through copper pillars, offering high bandwidth and low power.
Placing memory close to compute units to reduce data movement distance, improving bandwidth and energy efficiency.
Data movement capability becomes the performance bottleneck, so no matter how many compute cores there are, they can't be fully utilized.
A parallel processing architecture that can manage multiple sets of tasks simultaneously, improving compute unit utilization.

facts.k: Xuanjie O3 protocol conversion overhead reduction

quotes.text: Judging whether a company can really make chips, don't just stare at how many IPs it hand-built; you should look more at how much system definition power it holds.

Xiaomi isn't slowly learning to make chips; it's trading resources for time, and within a limited time window, building up as quickly as possible the complete capability station a mature chip company needs.
As long as data is stored reasonably and delivered efficiently, the entire chip can benefit from it.
Once it's done, there's no need to wait for a model defined by others, then use a generic chip to adapt, and then consider how to stuff it into a phone.
I'd rather bear more engineering and R&D uncertainty than wait until the window really closes and then regret not having walked a few steps faster.
